input:
When it comes to characterising a powder blend, it is tempting to assume that a material which has been thoroughly mixed will be uniform throughout, so that any small portion can be taken as representative of the whole. In practice, however, this assumption is unreliable, and great care has to be taken over how samples are obtained if the results are to mean anything.

The underlying difficulty is segregation. The particles that make up a blend differ in size and in density, and ordinary handling tends to separate them again: fine particles percolate downwards through the voids between coarser ones during transport and vibration, coarse particles roll outwards to the surface and the edges of a heap, and when a container is discharged the material does not leave uniformly from every region. The composition of the blend therefore varies from place to place, even in a batch that was well mixed to begin with.

For this reason, samples are built up from many increments taken at many points and at many times. Wherever the process permits, increments are cut from a moving stream across its full cross-section, on the grounds that such a cut gathers material that originated from all parts of the bed or vessel. Where the material is stationary, increments are drawn with a sampling thief from positions and depths spread across the whole mass, taking care that easily reached spots near walls and outlets do not dominate. All of the increments are combined into a single composite sample, and the laboratory portion is obtained from it by a splitting method, such as riffling, that does not select by particle size, so that local variations are averaged out.

A single grab sample, by contrast, can be seriously misleading, because it captures the composition of one location at one moment and silently presents it as the composition of the entire batch. The analysis itself may be perfectly accurate, yet the conclusion drawn from it wrong, since the error lies in the sampling rather than in the measurement. This discussion deliberately quotes no numerical limits: any limits that a sampling scheme has to meet are regulatory or contractual in nature, and they are set out in the site's permit rather than in a description of sampling practice.
target:
A powder blend is not uniform at the scale of a scoop. Particles differ in size and density, and handling moves them relative to each other: fine particles settle through voids during transport, coarse particles roll to the surface and to the edges of a heap, and discharge from a container draws material from some regions before others. A sample that is to stand for the whole batch must be built against that segregation.

Samples are therefore taken at many points and at many times rather than at one accessible point. Increments are drawn across the full cross-section of a moving stream where the process allows it, because a stream cut in passing contains material from every part of the bed or container that fed it. Where the material is at rest, increments are taken from distributed positions and depths with a sampling thief, and positions near walls and outlets are not allowed to dominate the set.

The increments are combined into one composite sample, which is then reduced to the laboratory portion by a method that does not select by particle size, such as riffling. Each increment contributes a small part of the whole, so the segregation of any one region is diluted by material from the rest of the batch, and the composite reports the batch average rather than any local composition.

A single grab sample misleads because it reports the composition of the place and moment it was taken from, generalised without warrant to the whole batch. In a segregated blend, that local composition can differ substantially from the batch average, and the error is invisible in the result itself: the analysis can be accurate for the scoop and wrong for the batch. No numerical limits are stated here. The limits a sampling scheme must satisfy are set by regulation or by contract, and they belong to the site's permit, not to the sampling method.
